name: Lipodissolve (phosphatidylcholine injections)

card.summary: Unapproved fat-dissolving injections of phosphatidylcholine and deoxycholate; small uncontrolled reports of fat reduction, no approved product, and documented infections and inflammation.
card.aka: Injection lipolysis, PC/DC injections, lipodissolve, mesotherapy for fat
card.note: Not an FDA-approved fat-reduction product; case reports describe infections and severe inflammation after injections.

quick.overview:
Lipodissolve, also called injection lipolysis, is a cosmetic procedure in which a mixture of phosphatidylcholine and the detergent sodium deoxycholate is injected into small pockets of fat. Practitioners who offer it say it shrinks localized fat and tightens skin, and it was marketed in the 2000s as a non-surgical alternative to liposuction.

Published support consists mostly of practitioner-authored reports and small studies. Reviews describe it as having drawn scrutiny from the media and the US Food and Drug Administration. A different deoxycholic-acid-only product, Kybella, was later approved by the FDA for fat under the chin, but that approval does not cover phosphatidylcholine mixtures.
quick.mechanism: Proponents proposed that phosphatidylcholine breaks down fat, while later reviews suggest the deoxycholate detergent action, which destroys fat cell membranes, may account for observed effects. The body then clears the released material over weeks.
quick.risks: Reported problems include pain, bruising, swelling, nodules, severe inflammation and infection, including a published case of mycobacterial infection after injections. Mixtures are often compounded rather than manufactured to an approved standard. The FDA has not approved phosphatidylcholine injections for fat reduction.

lead: Lipodissolve, also known as injection lipolysis or PC/DC injection, is a cosmetic procedure in which a mixture of phosphatidylcholine (PC) and sodium deoxycholate (DC) is injected into subcutaneous fat to reduce small localized deposits, such as under the chin, on the abdomen, flanks, thighs or upper arms. People seek it as a non-surgical way to slim a contour, and practitioners have described it as an adjunct to or alternative for liposuction in areas holding only small amounts of fat.[1][2][5]

The approach grew out of European and Brazilian practice. Phosphatidylcholine-based drugs had been used intravenously for fat embolism and lipid disorders, and a formulation sold in Germany as Lipostabil became the starting point for injecting fat directly.[2] The technique is often grouped with mesotherapy, although a 2006 review argued that traditional mesotherapy and phosphatidylcholine injections have different histories and should not be treated as synonyms.[3][4]

Published support comes mainly from practitioner series, including one describing 1,616 patients and 15,122 treatments, and from a placebo-controlled study of deoxycholate showing that it lyses fat cells and causes inflammation.[6][7] Regulators have taken a cautious line: the FDA sent warning letters in 2010 about marketing of lipodissolve products, and the FDA approved a purified deoxycholic acid product, Kybella, for chin fat in 2015, which is a separate product from PC/DC mixtures.[2][8]

paras: In the procedure a practitioner delivers a series of small injections of a compounded PC/DC solution into the target area over several sessions. Practitioner papers describe selecting patients with discrete pockets of fat, treating regions with defined spacing, and expecting swelling, tenderness and bruising afterward.[5][9] Practitioner authors state that it does not replace traditional liposuction and that results depend on the formula, the injection technique and patient selection.[1]

A solution of phosphatidylcholine in deoxycholate that evolved around 2004 was used by two collaborating Minnesota physicians whose experience is reported in a 2012 paper.[7] In Germany and Switzerland, the mixture is today compounded by pharmacies, according to Wikipedia.[2]

According to Wikipedia, investigators noted in 1966 that intravenous phosphatidylcholine solutions could clear fat emboli. A formulation named Lipostabil, containing 5% phosphatidylcholine and 2.5% deoxycholate, was later approved in Germany for conditions including fat embolism and dyslipidemia, and the first reported use of its injection for fat removal involved fat under the eyelid.[2]

Cosmetic use spread in Brazil and Europe and then reached the United States in the early 2000s, where it was marketed in medspas under the name lipodissolve. A 2006 Dermatologic Surgery review distinguished the Brazilian-popularized phosphatidylcholine injections from French mesotherapy and noted that safety and efficacy remained unclear to most patients and physicians.[3] A 2008 paper described the practice as growing rapidly and called for standards of practice on indications, contraindications and expected post-injection effects.[5] By 2011 a review noted that after initial enthusiasm earlier in the decade, these methods had come under critical scrutiny by the media and the FDA.[10]

Early proponents credited phosphatidylcholine with dissolving fat. Cell-culture work and later human work pointed to the detergent deoxycholate as an active agent, since it disrupts cell membranes.[4][8] In a study of 30 volunteers, injections of sodium deoxycholate produced dose-dependent adipocyte lysis, necrosis of fat tissue, an inflammatory infiltrate and phagocytosis of fat cells by macrophages, with fibrosis seen at six months; placebo injections caused no histologic change.[8]

A French author, writing after a year of use, suggested the procedure may be helpful in unfavorable indications for liposuction because of the inflammatory reaction that follows adipolysis, and stated it would not replace liposuction.[11]

Authors who practice the technique report reduced localized fat and skin retraction in areas with small deposits, cellulite or post-liposuction irregularities.[1] In the Minnesota experience, relatively modest injection volumes produced satisfactory and smooth results in 74.5 to 86.5 percent of patients in the two practices, with no serious complications reported in that series.[7]

Wikipedia notes that no placebo-controlled studies have demonstrated the safety or efficacy of PC/DC mixtures, while numerous retrospective studies of Lipostabil injections have reported efficacy.[2] A case report described a lipoma treated by injection lipolysis with no recurrence at nine months.[12] A review of liposuction technology described chemical lipolysis as an alternative for localized fat while noting that skepticism remains.[13]

Expected short-term effects include pain, heat, redness, swelling, bruising and nodules at injection sites.[5][8] Rarer events appear in case reports: a woman developed agitation and metabolic acidosis after a lipodissolve injection, and a 53-year-old woman developed painful mycobacterial nodules at arm injection sites.[14][9]

The FDA received reports of permanent scarring, skin deformation and deep painful knots after the procedure, according to Wikipedia's summary of its 2010 statement.[2] Three US medical societies (ASPS, ASAPS and ASDS) have issued health warnings about injection lipolysis, and in the UK the MHRA said products were being unlawfully advertised as cosmetic fat reducers.[2] Wikipedia's mesotherapy article records an Australian salon investigation in 2008 after clients developed skin abscesses.[15]

On April 7, 2010, the FDA issued warning letters to six US medspas and a Brazilian company for false or misleading website claims about lipodissolve, stating that the products were not approved for fat removal and that it knew of no clinical evidence supporting claims such as treating male breast enlargement or lipomas.[2] In the UK, doctors can still inject the mixture while it cannot be promoted as a fat-reduction drug, and the Medical Protection Society stopped offering malpractice cover for it from 2005.[2]

A German physician network reported by Wikipedia collected about 29,889 patient results across roughly 76,000 sessions in its 2015 Lipolysis Report, with 4% of members responding.[2] Deoxycholic acid alone (Kybella) was approved by the FDA in 2015 for moderate to severe submental fullness.[2][16]

A randomized study of 30 volunteers received four sessions of 1% or 2.5% sodium deoxycholate or placebo in the abdomen, with follow-up to six months; deoxycholate lysed fat cells in a dose-dependent way and caused inflammation, pain and nodules.[8] The Minnesota clinical series reported on 1,616 patients and 15,122 treatments, with satisfactory results in 74.5 to 86.5 percent.[7]

Registered studies include NCT00757081, a 2008 study of 20 participants on abdominal subcutaneous fat (completed), and NCT00851747, a 2009 study of 18 participants (terminated); results are not posted in the cited entries.[17][18] Practitioner reports describe fat reduction and skin retraction.[1]

Lipodissolve was promoted in the 2000s as a lunchtime alternative to liposuction. Forum discussions on T Nation mention injected compounds as a past route to spot fat loss, and one thread links to a clinic offering micro-injections of a soy-derived phosphatidylcholine compound for chest contouring.[19][20] In looksmaxxing circles, interest has shifted toward approved submental products and surgical options.

The simple PC-in-deoxycholate solution used in Minnesota practices evolves.[7]

lore.intro: Fat-dissolving injections are discussed in appearance forums as a non-surgical option for chin and body fat, often with disagreement about product quality and safety.

claims.claim: Lipodissolve melts localized fat without surgery
claims.believers: Practitioners and patients say injections reduce small fat pockets and tighten skin as an alternative to liposuction.[1][7]
claims.experts: Practitioner series report satisfaction, while Wikipedia notes no placebo-controlled study has shown efficacy of PC/DC mixtures; reviews note media and FDA scrutiny.[2][10]

claims.claim: Phosphatidylcholine is the active fat-dissolving ingredient
claims.believers: Marketing centered on phosphatidylcholine as a natural fat emulsifier.[1]
claims.experts: A randomized study found that deoxycholate alone lyses fat cells and causes inflammation.[8]

claims.claim: Compounded injections are as safe as approved products
claims.believers: Proponents say correct formula, technique and patient selection make the procedure safe, and one 1,616-patient series reported no serious complications.[1][7]
claims.experts: Case reports describe mycobacterial infection and metabolic acidosis, and the FDA warned about scarring and deep nodules.[9][14][2]
